records.text: 80. The Committee will establish and communicate the due date of the combined fifth to ninth periodic reports of the State Party in due course, in line with the envisaged predictable reporting calendar, and following the adoption of a list of issues and questions prior to reporting, if applicable, for the State Party. The reports should be in compliance with the Committee’s harmonized treaty-specific reporting guidelines and should not exceed 21,200 words. In the event that reports exceeding the established word limit is submitted, the State Party will be asked to shorten the reports. If the State Party is not in a position to review and resubmit the reports, translation thereof for the purposes of consideration by the Committee cannot be guaranteed.
themes: Cooperation & Follow up with Treaty Bodies

records.section: B. National mechanism for reporting and follow-up
records.text: 79. The Committee recommends that the State Party strengthen the Human Rights and Humanitarian Division under the Department of Multilateral Affairs of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as well as the policy and international divisions of the Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development, and ensure that they have the mandate and adequate human, technical and financial resources to coordinate and engage with, and prepare reports to, international and regional human rights mechanisms and to coordinate and track national follow-up to, and the implementation of, treaty obligations and the recommendations and decisions emanating from those mechanisms effectively. The Committee emphasizes that the Human Rights and Humanitarian Division should be adequately and continuously supported by dedicated staff and should have the capacity to consult systematically with the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia and civil society.

records.text: 78. The Committee recommends that the State Party take all appropriate measures to ensure that the recommendations contained in the present concluding observations are fully implemented and that a child-friendly version is disseminated to, and made widely accessible for, children, including those in the most disadvantaged situations. The Committee also recommends that the combined second to fourth periodic reports , the written replies to the list of issues and the present concluding observations be made widely available in the languages of the country.

records.text: 77. The Committee recommends that the State Party cooperate, among others, with the Commission on the Promotion and Protection of the Rights of Women and Children of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

records.section: M. Ratification of international human rights instruments
records.text: 76. The Committee recommends that the State Party, in order to further strengthen the fulfilment of children’s rights, consider ratifying the following core human rights instruments: (a) Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment; (b) International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights; (c) Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights; (d) Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming to the abolition of the death penalty; (e) International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination; (f) International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families.

records.text: 73. The Committee is concerned about the fact that the legal age of criminal responsibility is extremely low and, recalling its general comment No. 24 (2019) on children’s rights in the child justice system, the Committee urges the State Party to bring its child justice system fully into line with the Convention and other relevant international rules and principles. In particular, the Committee urges the State Party : (a) To raise the legal age of criminal responsibility to at least 14 years of age ; (b) To secure equal special protections and due process guarantees for all children before the High Court and for those accused jointly with adults; (c) To ensure the provision of free and specialized legal aid to children alleged as, accused of or recognized as having infringed criminal law at an early stage of the procedure and throughout the legal proceedings ; (d) To actively promote non-judicial measures , such as diversion and mediation, for children alleged as, accused of or recognized as having infringed criminal law and, wherever possible, the use of non-custodial sentences for children, such as probation or community service, and ensure that health and psychosocial services are provided to such children; (e) To ensure that detention is used only as a measure of last resort and for the shortest appropriate period of time and is reviewed on a regular basis with a view to the release of the child.
sdg_targets: 16.3: Promote the rule of law and access to justice for all

Recalling its general comment No. 11 (2009) on Indigenous children and their rights under the Convention , the Committee urges the State Party: (a) To consult and cooperate with Indigenous Peoples, including Indigenous children, in order to obtain their free, prior and informed consent before adopting and implementing legislative or administrative measures that may affect them, and provide effective remedies in cases of violations of their rights; (b) To cooperate with Indigenous authorities to adopt a national policy and action plan and provide the necessary resources for Indigenous children to enjoy a decent standard of living and their right to decide their own development policies in their traditionally inhabited territories and in accordance with their culture and spiritual beliefs.

records.text: 67. Recalling the joint general comments No. 3 and No. 4 of the Committee on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families/No. 22 and No. 23 of the Committee on the Rights of the Child (2017) on the human rights of children in the context of international migration , the Committee reiterates its previous recommendations and recommends that the State Party: (a) Amend the Immigration Act, 1959–1963, the Child Act, 2001, and related policies to end the immigration detention of children; (b) End the detention of asylum-seeking, refugee and migrant families with children to prevent the separation of children and accelerate the implementation of alternatives to detention, prioritizing family-based and community-based options; (c) Ensure that migrant children are not detained on the basis of their or their parents’ migration status and that alternatives to detention are available; (d) Ensure access for refugee, asylum-seeking, migrant, undocumented and stateless children to legal protection and public education, health and other basic services; (e) Remove any regulation, such as the Ministry of Health directive (circular No. 10/2001), that requires healthcare personnel to report undocumented persons and establish a firewall policy between service providers and the immigration authorities.

records.text: 62. Recalling its general comment No. 26 (2023) on children’s rights and the environment, with a special focus on climate change , the Committee recommends that the State Party: (a) Ensure that children’s special vulnerabilities, needs and views are taken into account in policies environmental and climate policies, such as the second national climate change policy and the national disaster risk reduction policy, 2030 ; (b) Strengthen the mechanisms for the participation of children in climate change and environmental policies, such as the Youth Climate Adaptation Forum; (c) Increase children’s awareness and preparedness for climate change and natural disasters by incorporating it into the school curriculum and teacher training programmes; (d) Strengthen the disaster response by expanding child-friendly temporary evacuation centres that are equipped to provide psychological and medical support.

Recalling its general comment No. 4 (2003) on adolescent health and development in the context of the Convention and general comment No. 20 (2016) on the implementation of the rights of the child during adolescence, the Committee recommends that the State Party : (a) Adopt a comprehensive sexual and reproductive health policy for adolescents and ensure that sexual and reproductive health education is part of the mandatory school curriculum and targeted at adolescents, with special attention given to preventing early pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections; (b) Decriminalize abortion in all circumstances and ensure access to safe abortion and post-abortion care services for adolescent girls, making sure that their views are always heard and given due consideration as a part of the decision-making process; (c) Develop and implement a policy to protect the rights of pregnant teenagers, adolescent mothers and their children, including against discrimination ; (d) Address the prevalence of drug use among children by expanding accessible and child-friendly drug dependence treatment, including in care institutions.

records.section: Children deprived of a family environment
records.text: 51. Drawing the State Party’s attention to the Guidelines for the Alternative Care of Children, the Committee recommends that the State Party : (a) Phase out institutionalization and adopt, without delay, a strategy and action plan for deinstitutionalization, drawing from pilot experiences and ensuring that it has the adequate human, technical and financial resources for its implementation and includes the systemic transformation of the childcare, welfare and protection systems; (b) Conduct a comprehensive mapping of all care institutions, including those that are not registered, as a basis for strengthening the registration and monitoring system, ensuring quality standards of care , including reasonable accommodation, and monitoring the situation of children placed in these institutions; (c) Strengthen the capacity of the Department of Social Welfare, in coordination with other relevant regulatory authorities, to conduct regular inspections and enforce compliance with the Care Centre Act and Regulations, 1993; (d) Step up efforts to ensure sufficient family-based, community-based and foster care options for children who cannot stay with their families; (e) Strengthen the capacity of professionals and others working with families and children to enhance their awareness of the rights and needs of children deprived of a family environment.

The Committee is concerned about the following: (a) Lack of information about the number of children in non-registered institutional care and the lack of safeguards on both registered and non-registered institutional care, placing children at risk of abuse, neglect and sexual abuse and exploitation; (b) Insufficient capacity of the Department of Social Welfare to register and monitor registered and non-registered institutions; (c) Reports of the prevalence of children with disabilities in institutional care and lack of reasonable accommodation in these institutions; (d) Insufficiency of foster care and family-based alternative care.

The Committee draws the State Party’s attention to its statement on article 5 of the Convention and recommends that the State Party: (a) Adopt measures for the effective implementation of the Child (Family ‐ Based Care) Regulation, 2017; (b) Ensure that mothers and fathers share the responsibility for their children equally, in accordance with article 18 (1) of the Convention ; (c) Adopt family-friendly policies, such as paid parental leave, breastfeeding breaks and childcare, that support women, working families and caregivers.

records.text: 47. Recalling joint general recommendation No. 31 of the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women/general comment No. 18 of the Committee on the Rights of the Child (2019) on harmful practices, the Committee urges the State Party: (a) To urgently unify the minimum legal age of marriage at 18 years, without exception, in civil law, sharia law and customary law; (b) To assess the national strategic plan for handling the causes of child marriages (2022–2025) and update it with the meaningful participation of children, in particular girls; (c) To expand public awareness-raising programmes on the harmful effects of child marriage on the physical and mental health and well-being of girls; (d) To establish a national child protection framework, including integrated data collection that includes all forms of marriage of those under 18 years of age, the mandatory monitoring of child marriage cases, independent oversight and child ‐ friendly justice mechanisms; (e) To undertake a study on female genital mutilation, including its acceptance in the context of cultural norms and religious beliefs; (f) To prohibit female genital mutilation in civil law, sharia law and customary law; (g) To set up strategies and mechanisms for data collection on female genital mutilation and for providing medical and psychological support to victims, as well as access to justice and remedies; (h) To prohibit non-urgent and non-essential medical or surgical treatment, including the feminizing or masculinizing of intersex children before they are of sufficient age or maturity to make their own decision and provide their free, prior and informed consent; (i) To provide social, medical and psychological services, as well as adequate counselling and support, to intersex children and their families.

Noting the adoption of the national strategic plan for handling the causes of child marriages (2022–2025), the Committee remains deeply concerned about the following: (a) Persistence of child marriage and that, while the minimum age for marriage is set at 18 under civil law, it is allowed for those under 18 years of age under sharia law and is undetermined in customary law; (b) Practice of female genital mutilation, the lack of its explicit prohibition by law, the medicalization of the procedure leading to increasing harmful female genital mutilation and the lack of data on its prevalence; (c) Prevalence of the medical and religious approaches to intersex children and the permissibility of medically unnecessary surgeries and other procedures on intersex children, which often entail irreversible consequences and can cause severe physical and psychological suffering.

Recalling its general comment No. 8 (2006) on the right of the child to protection from corporal punishment and other cruel or degrading forms of punishment, the Committee reiterates its previous recommendations and urges the State Party: (a) To explicitly prohibit corporal punishment in all settings in homes, public and religious schools ( tahfiz ), childcare institutions, alternative care settings and penal institutions; (b) To repeal sections 78 and 89 of the Penal Code (Act No. 574 of 1997), sections 288 and 293 of the Criminal Procedure Code, section 50 of the Prison Act, 1995, as well as all other norms in the Education Act, 1996, the Child Act, 2001, and sharia law that allow for corporal punishment; (c) To promote positive, non-violent and participatory forms of child-rearing and discipline.

records.section: Abuse, neglect, sexual abuse and exploitation
records.text: 43. While noting the establishment of child welfare teams mandated to coordinate the provision of local services, the Committee reiterates its previous recommendations and, i n the light of its general comment No. 13 (2011) on the right of the child to freedom from all forms of violence , recommends that the State Party : (a) Ensure the effective implementation of the Domestic Violence Act, 1994, and the Sexual Offences Against Children Act, 2017, as well as the Child Act, 2001, to protect all children regardless of their legal status in the State Party; (b) Develop and adopt a national strategy on violence against children with the meaningful participation of children from all backgrounds; (c) Strengthen the child protection system to ensure its effectiveness, notably by ensuring intersectoral coordination, nationwide coverage and case management, including in the digital environment, and provide sufficient human, technical and financial resources; (d) Adopt without further delay the social work profession bill, ensuring that it includes all social workers in the child protection system, including from the public sector; (e) Ensure that all cases of child abuse, including sexual abuse, are promptly reported and investigated, applying a child-friendly and multisectoral approach, with the aim of avoiding the revictimization of the child, that perpetrators are prosecuted and duly sanctioned and that reparations are provided to victims, as appropriate; (f) Fully operationalize the amended Evidence of Child Witness Act, 2007, and develop guidelines on child-friendly forensic interviews for all proceedings ; (g) Allocate sufficient resources to the provision of child-friendly and comprehensive support, including trauma-focused therapy, to children who are victims, promote alternative family-based and community-based care options and prohibit the placement of children in centres that accommodate adults; (h) Establish a new national child-friendly helpline for children, with a single, three-digit, toll-free number, operating 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and provide it with the necessary human, financial and technical resources for its effective functioning ; (i) Adopt measures to address and prevent bullying in all settings, including against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex children ; (j) Adopt legislation that prohibits the sale of children, including in the digital environment.

Recalling its general comment No. 25 (2021) and the 2026 joint statement of the Committee and other signing parties on artificial intelligence and the rights of the child , the Committee recommends that the State Party: (a) Adopt a child rights-based approach to the implementation of the Online Safety Act, 2025; (b) Ensure that children are adequately protected from harmful content and materials and online risks and provide for mechanisms to prosecute violations; (c) Continue to improve digital inclusion for children in disadvantaged situations and living in remote areas, with accessible and affordable online services; (d) Adopt culturally sensitive measures to ensure the digital inclusion of children living in rural areas of East Malaysia and Indigenous children in West Malaysia; (e) Scale up the measures taken to enhance the digital literacy and skills of children, teachers and families, including on online risks and safeguards; (f) Elaborate regulations on artificial intelligence in the context of the rights of the child, with a view to ensuring the acceleration of opportunities and protecting them from harm.

Recalling its general comment No. 25 (2021) on children’s rights in relation to the digital environment, it recommends that the State Party apply a child rights-based approach in the implementation of the Online Safety Act, 2025, to ensure the protection of children’s right to privacy and provide for mechanisms to prosecute violations.

records.section: Freedom of expression, religion, association and peaceful assembly
records.text: 39. The Committee urges the State Party: (a) To review the Sedition Act, 1948, and section 233 of the Communication and Multimedia Act, 1998, to ensure that children feel safe to express their opinions and are free from censorship, surveillance, intimidation, harassment, bullying and cyberbullying; (b) To strengthen children’s right to freedom of association and peaceful assembly, including by removing age-limit restrictions from the Peaceful Assembly Act, 2012; (c) To ensure that the measures adopted to address interfaith disputes and religious conversion practices do respect children’s freedom of religion.

records.text: 84. The ageing population of Malaysia presents both challenges and opportunities. The widespread awareness within the Government about that fact constitutes an excellent starting point for adapting to the changing demographics and fulfilling the human rights of older persons. The current efforts, however, largely lack a cohesive, human rights-based and systematic approach. Collecting data disaggregated by age and making them freely availab le to both the public and government institutions remain area s requiring urgent attention to ensure public discussion and effective policymaking. In summary, the Government must transition from recognizing ageing as a priority to formulating and implementing rights-based policies. The vibrant civil society of Malaysia, the groundbreaking work of academia in the country on the topic of ageing and committed public officials are excellent assets for that important task. 85. The Government affirmed its opposition to discrimination, emphasizing that its policies were inclusive and that services were open to all. It must recognize, however, that addressing discrimination effectively requires a targeted approach that takes into account the specific needs of each affected group, particularly those experiencing multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination. General assertions of inclusivity and openness are insufficient to ensure substantive equality. In the case of older persons, confronting structural ageism is essential in order to move beyond formal equality and ensure that laws, services and public discourse reflect their lived realities and human rights.

records.text: 79. The Independent Expert met with officials of the Ministry of Digital, created in December 2023, who acknowledged the existence of a digital gap affecting older persons and their rights, including the right to access to public information in the digital sphere. They did not provide specific data on the extent of the gap, however, nor any targeted strategy to bridge it, other than the measures targeting the gap in the general population. 80. Policy documents shared with the Independent Expert confirmed the lack of focus on older persons, including the Malaysia Digital Economy Blueprint of 2021 and the Ministry’s latest flagship initiative, AI for Rakyat (Artificial Intelligence for the People). While one of the objectives for the blueprint is bridging the digital gap, older persons are not mentioned in it. AI for Rakyat is aimed at the following age groups: 0 to 18 years, 18 to 35 years, 35 to 50 years and over 50 years. The fact that all persons above the age of 50 are categorized in a single group dilutes the specific needs of older persons in their 60s, 70s and 80s. It can be assumed that the digital gap is the most acute among the oldest generations of Malaysia. 81. On a positive note, the Ministry of Digital offers specific activities for older persons relating to scam prevention as part of its CyberSAFE (Cyber Security Awareness for Everyone) programme. Older persons need to be seen as active citizens who can contribute to society in the digital sphere, not only as potential victims of cybercrime. After the visit, the Ministry of Digital shared with the Independent Expert its plans to establish a digital inclusion index to assess and bridge the digital divide, particularly among older persons, by analysing data on accessibility, affordability, digital literacy and age-friendly technology. 82. The Independent Expert was informed of several positive practices. In Penang, the local council had designed, in cooperation with older persons, an application offering information on the local community and public services. Thanks to the participation of older persons, the designers had incorporated their suggestions, using, for example, colours selected by older persons that facilitated readability. The application also included, as suggested by older persons, an SOS button that enabled direct requests for emergency services. 83. In George Town, older persons are taught digital skills by other older persons who are technology experts in an activity centre administered by a non-governmental organization. The peer-to-peer learning has proved itself to be better adapted to their needs and communication style than similar programmes taught by younger persons.

records.text: 75. The Independent Expert visited several Pusat Aktiviti Warga Emas (Golden Citizen Activity Centres) for older persons, which are focused on older persons’ right to participate in the cultural life of the community and promote an active lifestyle. The centres visited included those managed by the federal and state governments and non-governmental organizations. They all offered a wide range of social, cultural and sports activities in positive and encouraging environments. 76. The Independent Expert noted that shortcomings prevented a wider impact, however, with the centres using an approach that was insufficiently human rights-based. The facilities that she observed had visible physical barriers affecting those with limited mobility and the activities lacked adapted content for those with visual or hearing disabilities. Government-provided data show that 210 older persons with disabilities are users of the Pusat Aktiviti Warga Emas network, a seemingly low number considering the existence of 168 centres. In addition, despite the annual public allocation of 50,000 Malaysian ringgit (approximately $11,000) to each centre, added to a one-time grant of 100,000 Malaysian ringgit (approximately $22,000) soon to be established for newly opened centres, users have to pay fees, which may exclude older persons with lower incomes. 77. Many Pusat Aktiviti Warga Emas have a strong religious focus, potentially excluding non-religious older persons or those belonging to religions other than the majority religion in the area in which the centre is located. Those factors diminish the appeal of the centres for the extremely diverse older population of Malaysia, despite being, as volunteers supporting the centres insisted, “open to all”. 78. The Independent Expert positively acknowledges the participation of many Malaysian entities in the World Health Organization Global Network for Age-friendly Cities and Communities, which is aimed at strengthening accessibility and social inclusion for older persons in the community through support for volunteering and cooperation with the communal authorities. Communities implementing the Age-friendly Cities Framework include Ipoh, Kuching, Penang Island, Petaling Jaya, Taiping and Sibu.

records.text: Older LGBTQI+ persons 67. The Independent Expert heard compelling testimonies showing that older LGBTQI+ persons in Malaysia faced multifaceted and compound human rights challenges caused by criminalization, discrimination, exclusion from legal protections and systemic neglect. The intersection of age, gender identity and sexual orientation significantly exacerbated those challenges. The Independent Expert was particularly alarmed by the situation of older transgender women, who endured social isolation, health inequities, economic hardship and exposure to harmful practices sponsored by the Government. 68. The legal and socioreligious landscape of Malaysia galvanizes systemic discrimination towards LGBTQI+ persons, which does not diminish for LGBTQI+ persons in older age. For example, sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code ban consensual intercourse between adults, as do sharia law provisions in several states. Together with section 21 of the Minor Offences Act 1955 (revised 1987), which prohibits drunkenness and disorderly behaviour in public places, that legislation has historically been used to criminalize and harass LGBTQI+ persons, with a particularly harmful impact on transgender women. Civil society organizations have documented that reports of police abuse, arbitrary detention and the denial of medical care during incarceration, particularly during the 1980s and 1990s, remain unresolved and inadequately investigated and continue to affect older transgender women victims. The Government stated that the Royal Malaysia Police had not received such cases. 69. The federal and state-level criminalization of consensual same-sex relations continues to violate the sexual rights of older LGBTQI+ persons. The negative human rights impact of criminalizing consensual same-sex relations has long been established in the United Nations human rights system. The Human Rights Committee has found a violation of the right to privacy by that type of legislation, irrespective of its enforcement. Several special procedure mandate holders have also found a link between criminalization and homophobic hate crimes, torture and family and community violence. In that regard, the Special Rapporteur on the right of everyone to the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health found during his 2014 visit to Malaysia that the criminalization of same-sex conduct reinforced negative societal attitudes and led to serious human rights violations, including barriers in access to healthcare. He recommended that the country decriminalize sodomy and remove any legal provisions that criminalized same-sex conduct and different forms of gender identity and expression. 70. Another aspect of the legal framework negatively affecting the rights of older LGBTQI+ persons is the lack of legal gender recognition for transgender persons in Malaysia, which creates systemic barriers in access to services and protections. In addition, the Constitution and anti-discrimination legislation do not include sexual orientation and gender identity as prohibited grounds of discrimination, and same-sex marriages and intimate partnerships are not recognized by law. 71. Older LGBTQI+ persons often experience estrangement from their biological families due to stigma and rejection. As a result, many rely on an intimate partner and “chosen families” – networks of close friends, partners and community members – for emotional support, caregiving and end-of-life decisions. Legislation in Malaysia, however, does not recognize same-sex civil unions or domestic partnerships and largely fails to recognize those ties, thereby excluding same-sex intimate partners and chosen families from critical decisions and entitlements, such as inheritance rights, hospital visitation, health proxies and next-of-kin recognition. That denies older LGBTQI+ persons the rights to dignity, care and autonomy at moments in life in which they may be at their most vulnerable. 72. Healthcare systems in Malaysia often fail to provide for older transgender and gender-diverse persons, who report delays, denials and mistreatment in healthcare settings. Their mental health issues, which are compounded by historical trauma and stigma, are widespread and underaddressed, according to information received by the Independent Expert. 73. Lifelong employment discrimination leaves many older LGBTQI+ persons without sufficient retirement savings, social security or insurance. Many do not have access to public social protection systems due to stigma, bureaucratic barriers or fear of State reprisal. 74. The Independent Expert also received information on government-sponsored programmes, such as “Mukhayyam” camps, which use religious shame, coercion and incentives to “convert” or “rehabilitate” LGBTQI+ persons. Older individuals, especially those who are socially and economically disadvantaged, are more vulnerable to such practices and disproportionately pressured into participation. The Government assured the Independent Expert that the Mukhayyam programme was strictly voluntary and respected the dignity of LGBTQI+ persons. Practices based on the belief that a person’s sexual orientation and gender identity and expression can and must be changed or suppressed can constitute torture. The Independent Expert received information that, during the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic, State aid was selectively distributed to LGBTQI+ persons who complied with conversion programmes, excluding many in need.

records.text: 59. Indigenous Peoples in Malaysia, who constitute heterogeneous populations, are grouped by the Government into two distinct categories: Orang Asli in Peninsular Malaysia, comprising around 18 ethnic groups, and Natives in Borneo, comprising over 80 ethnic groups. According to a 2021 report by the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia, the rights of Indigenous Peoples are negatively affected by poverty, a lower life expectancy, a lack of basic access to education, healthcare, sanitation and infrastructure and inadequate legislation and policies on land rights. 60. Government policy is also jeopardized by the lack of data on older Indigenous persons. For instance, the Independent Expert enquired about the life expectancy of Indigenous persons to compare it with that of the general population. The Government responded, however, that the only data available for the life expectancy of Indigenous Peoples referred to the Bumiputera, a term that included both Indigenous Peoples and the ethnic Malay population, the non-Indigenous and politically and economically dominant ethnic group in the country. The Government stated that the life expectancy of that group was 72 years for males and 76.5 years for females, roughly the same as for the general population: 73 years for males and 77.8 years for females. Those figures contradicted research indicating the life expectancy of Indigenous Malaysians to be around 16 years shorter than that of the general population. 61. Despite the Independent Expert’s intention to visit Indigenous territories and directly observe the living conditions of older Indigenous persons in rural or remote areas, the short time available for planning the visit made that impossible. The Independent Expert talked to older Indigenous representatives of different states, however, and received vivid and detailed accounts of their situation and their difficulties in fully enjoying their human rights on an equal basis with the wider Malaysian society. 62. Many older Indigenous persons have worked only in agriculture, without formal employment, leaving them without any income after retirement. Traditionally, families have provided for older Indigenous persons but they are under severe strain, mainly as a result of the migration of younger generations, both internally and internationally, and struggle to ensure older persons’ well-being. When older Indigenous persons do receive a pension or a social allowance, they are often pressured to share it with their extended families. 63. The situation of nomadic Indigenous Peoples is particularly concerning. They face barriers in their rights to education and social protection, with settling in a fixed location (and thus renouncing their right to keep their culture) the only avenue for them to enjoy economic and social rights. For example, there is no adaptation of public education for nomadic children, negatively affecting multiple human rights throughout their lives, nor is social support provided to older nomadic persons. 64. Many older nomadic persons lack birth certificates and are thus considered stateless, which deprives them of virtually all their human rights. Their right to freely move in the national territory is jeopardized due to their fear of arrest if they are found by the police or immigration authorities not to be in possession of a valid identification document. With hospitals located in major towns, they are inaccessible to many older nomadic persons, who fear travelling to urban areas due to the presence of the police. It is especially alarming that the descendants of the ancestral inhabitants of the present-day territory of Malaysia, many of whom are older persons, are unable to move freely within the country or have access to basic services due to the risk of arrest stemming from their undocumented status. Statelessness is often inherited by children born to stateless parents, perpetuating a cycle of exclusion that extends to older persons. The Government does not collect data on older stateless people, making it difficult to assess the extent of the issue and develop policies to ensure their rights. 65. Older Indigenous persons informed the Independent Expert that the lack of access to justice in land disputesin both cases of conflict among Indigenous Peoples and with government and private actors gravely affected their rights to life and security. Generally, there were no legal provisions that provided recognition of the land rights of Indigenous Peoples in Peninsular Malaysia. In Sabah and Sarawak, legislation recognized certain customary land rights, but itsimplementationwas still lacking. 66. A good practice shared with the Independent Expert was the provision to remote Indigenous communities of public information via radio and television in their own languages, an initiative with a particularly positive impact on older Indigenous persons, who were often reliant on those types of communications.

records.text: 49. The Independent Expert visited Kamunting Correctional Centre in Perak, where she obtained valuable information on the efforts made by the Government to improve the situation of older persons in detention through a pilot programme known as Mentari (Sunshine). The visit allowed the Independent Expert to highlight aspects of the pilot programme that could be improved, enabling it to contribute substantially to the human rights of older persons in detention throughout Malaysia. 50. The Mentari programme had established a separate ward for older men, offering 38 older men an area segregated from the general prison population and contributing to their tranquillity and protection from the risk of abuse by younger prisoners. 51. The inmates interviewed by the Independent Expert invariably said that they were treated with respect. Positively, the ward addressed the religious diversity of its residents, facilitating prayer, religious training, activities and specific diets for Muslims, Christians and Buddhists. It also offered access to a fruit and vegetable garden, improving prisoners’ mental and physical well-being and enriching their diets. 52. The Independent Expert observed, however, several aspects that constituted discrimination against older persons as outlined in the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Nelson Mandela Rules). For example, showing an ageist bias, older persons were told by prison officials that they were too old and frail to receive vocational training or have access to employment in prison. Detainees who were trained and experienced in carpentry and willing and able to work, for example, were not allowed to work in the prison carpentry workshop. The only older detainee who was employed received a salary of only between 0.30 and 0.60 Malaysian ringgit (approximately $0.7 to $0.14) per day. Prison officials stated that that amount (equally applied to the rest of the prison population) did not constitute a salary but an incentive. The motivating value of a monthly stipend of around $2 to $3 per month is questionable, however, and may constitute exploitation. As an example, buying a pot of precooked noodles, a popular item at the prison store, costs around $1.30. The minimum monthly salary in Malaysia stands at around $384. 53. Older persons in the Mentari ward also lacked sufficient activities. They organized themselves in the morning for light exercise but did not have a coach to instruct and motivate them, depending only on their own experience and initiative to promote that activity. They were also excluded from using the sports field in the prison, which the general population enjoyed about once per week. Walking is an activity that is especially suitable for older persons, but the Mentari ward lacked enough space for walking for exercise, an activity that would benefit the physical and mental health of older persons in detention if they had access to the sports field. 54. Older persons in the Mentari ward did enjoy enough access to safe drinking water, but the quality and amount of food provided was reportedly insufficient, with detainees interviewed by the Independent Expert stating that they were going hungry. Older persons who had money sent by their families bought instant noodles or other types of food in the prison store to complement their diets. 55. Access to medical check-ups and consultations were provided regularly to older persons in prison. The Independent Expert observed only one person with eyeglasses, however, out of 38 in the ward, a notably low number for a population of 38 men above the age of 60. Prison officials acknowledged that the welfare services lacked funding to provide inmates with eyeglasses. With reading and watching television as the main sources of entertainment, eyecare could be a critical factor for the well-being of older persons in the Mentari ward. Dental care was also insufficient, with no funds available at the time of the visit to provide older persons with dentures. According to the Government, the cost of eyeglasses, dental care and prosthetics was normally covered by families, civil society organizations or, in the case of foreign prisoners, embassies. 56. Another aspect where conditions in the Mentari ward fell below international standards was the visit regime. The stay in prison was divided into four stages. Advancing from one to the next was dependent on the good behaviour of the inmate. In the first stage, older persons were allowed only one visit per month, as an incentive to advance to the next stage. That highly restricted regime could violate the right of older persons in the early stages of incarceration to maintain their family relations, which should be guaranteed to all prisoners and not constitute a privilege earned by good behaviour. Rule 43 (3) of the Nelson Mandela Rules states that disciplinary sanctions or restrictive measures should not include the prohibition of family contact, and that contact may only be restricted for a limited time period and as strictly required for the maintenance of security and order. In addition, some of the detainees had been transferred against their will from locations that were four or five hours away from Kamunting by car, making it impossible for their families to visit them regularly. That severely affected their capacity to maintain family ties. Rule 59 of the Nelson Mandela Rules provides that prisoners be allocated, to the extent possible, to prisons close to their homes. 57. The Independent Expert acknowledges that it is not easy to achieve the right balance between the need for special wards for older persons, both men and women, and the need for prisoners to live as close to their homes as possible, and that the number of detainees is too low in smaller prisons for a special, dedicated ward. 58. Some of the older persons in detention interviewed by the Independent Expert had received lengthy prison sentences for drug-use offences under the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 (Act 234). As prison officials acknowledged to the Independent Expert, incarceration was not the most appropriate means to support persons who used drugs in terms of addressing their health and addiction-related needs. The Kamunting prison lacked specific treatments, even though the Government informed the Independent Expert that it offered rehabilitation programmes in prisons to persons who used drugs.

records.text: 37. The public healthcare system of Malaysia is funded by the public budget, and charges Malaysian citizens reduced fees for outpatient consultations (1 Malaysian ringgit (approximately $0.23) for general consultations, 5 Malaysian ringgit (approximately $1.12) for specialized care) at public health centres. Older persons enjoy a set of advantages in the public healthcare system: they have priority lines in all public hospitals and a system of staggered appointments to reduce multiple visits to healthcare centres. Most importantly, they are exempted from paying consultation fees, although they may be charged a reduced fee of up to 250 Malaysian ringgit (approximately $56) for hospitalization. While the fees for hospitalization may be a barrier for many older persons, the Independent Expert was assured by public officials that no Malaysian older person would be denied medical care for being unable to pay. Healthcare professionals, however, said that that statement was based on practice and not on official regulations. 38. Regrettably, the entitlements mentioned in the previous paragraph do not apply to persons who are not citizens of Malaysia, even migrants with a regularized situation in the country. The Independent Expert visited a public healthcare centre in Penang State, where the prices for consultations for different groups of people were visible on a board at the entrance. General consultations were 20 and 40 times more expensive for refugees and non-citizens, respectively. Specialized consultations were 12 and 24 times more expensive for the same groups. Older migrants and refugees needed to pay those fees as opposed to Malaysian older persons, who enjoyed free consultations. 39. The situation is even more dire for older stateless persons, a group that includes migrants, refugees, asylum-seekers and Malaysians who are unable to provide birth certificates to prove their nationality, such as Indigenous Peoples living in remote areas, some of them nomadic. Not only are they not entitled to the free healthcare enjoyed by older Malaysians with identity documents but they fear arrest if they go to healthcare facilities because of their undocumented status. As set out in its circular 10/2001, the Ministry of Health requires healthcare personnel to report undocumented persons when they seek treatment, a particularly concerning measure that exacerbates the vulnerable situation of older persons lacking identity documents. As a result, the Independent Expert heard accounts of older Indigenous persons postponing treatment for cancer and other serious diseases because of the risk of arrest. 40. The Independent Expert received reports of discrimination in the context of healthcare against older Indigenous persons, older persons of Indian descent and older LGBTQI+ persons. Public officials across the health sector shared with the Independent Expert their commitment to be “open for all”. They did not acknowledge, however, the existence of discrimination nor did they indicate any measures to prevent it. Healthcare personnel lacked training on ageism, ethnic discrimination and discrimination against LGBTQI+ persons. Fighting discriminatory biases embedded in society requires acknowledging the existence of those biases and working specifically towards their eradication. 41. In a positive development, LGBTQI+ persons interviewed by the Independent Expert mentioned that certain healthcare facilities had staff who were trained and sensitized on their situation and provided them with dignified treatment, making those facilities much-needed safe spaces. 42. Officials from different institutions pointed to the lack of a sufficient number of geriatricians as an obstacle to the enjoyment of the right to healthcare by older persons. There are only 68 qualified geriatricians working in Malaysia (38 in public hospitals and 30 in private hospitals), despite international standards requiring a minimum of 600 in relation to the country’s population of older persons. To reach that minimum, the number of medical students choosing geriatrics as a specialty needs to increase urgently. 43. The Independent Expert also received information on the difficulties for nurses to obtain one-year post-basic geriatric training due to the insufficient number of educational institutions providing it and the inability of most nurses to obtain leave in order to attend the training. According to government data, two training institutes belonging to the Ministry of Health award an advanced diploma in gerontology to around 60 nurses per year, an insufficient number for the country’s increasing demand. 44. The Government shared with the Independent Expert its multiple efforts to extend and strengthen the network of healthcare centres and hospitals in the entire country and to make them accessible to all older persons, including those living in remote areas. A positive example shared was the adaptation by the Penang Health Department of its community healthcare centres, formerly focused on child and maternal health, to become well-being centres for older persons where they could routinely receive health screenings and other health-related services. 45. Another positive development was the pilot project to provide online consultations for older patients in remote areas or for those not mobile enough to go to clinics. Online consultations can make healthcare accessible but can also present difficulties for those who are not digitally literate or lack the requisite equipment or access to the Internet due to cost or because they live in areas with reduced connectivity. In addition, online consultations cannot be used systematically as a substitute for physical interaction with healthcare providers, since in-person interaction can be essential for medical staff to individually assess the health and well-being of older patients and for older persons to benefit from personal interaction with healthcare providers. 46. Access to medication prescribed by doctors in the public health system is regularly provided without any additional cost for older persons, except to the groups mentioned above (migrants, refugees, asylum-seekers and stateless persons), who have to pay the full price or, in certain cases for registered refugees, a discounted 50 per cent of the price. Prescriptions are provided for one month and can be extended and sent via postal services, if needed. 47. Despite the efforts described in the previous paragraphs, older persons living in rural and remote areas, including Indigenous persons, often face significant obstacles in obtaining access to both primary and secondary healthcare, with long travel times and high travel-related expenses due to the lack of infrastructure. 48. The Independent Expert was also informed that, even though they remained unaffordable to most older persons, some people subscribed to private health insurance schemes in order to avoid the long waiting lists in public healthcare. The cost of private health insurance, however, had recently doubled or tripled in many cases, forcing many to cancel their subscriptions and lose private coverage. Many older persons shared with the Independent Expert that medicines prescribed in the private system were expensive and that they struggled to afford them.

records.text: 31. Families are the main institution providing long-term care to older persons in Malaysia. Many interlocutors, however, informed the Independent Expert that the family structure was slowly changing in the country, especially in rural areas, mostly due to the migration of the younger population to cities or third countries in search of better work opportunities. Decreased fertility and the rapidly advancing demographic shift have also jeopardized traditional family support systems. 32. The Independent Expert was informed that the care economy was a policy priority for the Government, to be addressed in the national ageing blueprint, an initiative of the Ministry of Economy to be published in July 2025. The Independent Expert was not provided with a copy of the draft but was informed that the blueprint would be aimed at building a sustainable long-term care system, reforming social protection, improving fiscal stability, promoting inclusive employment and education, combating ageism, fostering older persons’ societal participation, ensuring age-friendly infrastructure and supporting healthy, dignified ageing. The Independent Expert notes that she was not consulted on the document during the visit, when it was being drafted, which would have offered a suitable opportunity for technical cooperation and for the integration of a human rights-based and person-centred approach. 33. Malaysia has both public and private care homes, but the Independent Expert’s visit was focused on the public system. The public care home system has two different regimes in place: one focused on social support and another on providing healthcare. Private care homes need to be formally registered. The Independent Expert was informed, however, that many operated unregistered, out of reach of monitoring by the Government and possibly not compliant with minimum standards. The Government informed the Independent Expert of ongoing efforts to curb the widespread occurrence of unregistered care homes. The Department of Social Welfare was implementing a phased enforcement task force operation targeting such facilities across the country, which had undertaken enforcement actions against 1,028 homes and identified an additional 250 for planned enforcement action. 34. The Ministry of Human Resources has created occupational skills standards for jobs relating to the care of older persons and has certified 25 training centres that have so far trained 437 individuals on two curricula: Residential Care Activities for the Elderly and Disabled and Social Work Activities without Accommodation for the Elderly and Disabled. The curricula are not yet compulsory, however, for carrying out care work, resulting in a lack of common standards on quality of care. The existence of only those two curricula also indicates that there is no system in place to provide community-based care. 35. The fact that most older persons in Malaysia are still supported and cared for in family settings makes it necessary to provide sufficient training and support services to family caregivers, many of whom are older women themselves. That need is becoming even more critical with increasing longevity and the lack of public and private community-based support systems. 36. One of the public care homes visited by the Independent Expert, created to host older persons in poverty who had been abandoned, had no permanent domicile or had no family members to support them, showed the shortcomings of the common one-size-fits-all approach to older persons living in care homes. Instead of responding to the needs of each individual older person, the facility banned residents from leaving the premises at any time of day without previous authorization and being accompanied by a relative or staff member, which unduly restricted their right to liberty and freedom of movement and prevented them from enjoying the social and cultural life of the local community.

records.text: 28. The social protection system for older persons in Malaysia is characterized by fragmentation across multiple ministries, departments and agencies, each overseeing different aspects of welfare, healthcare, housing and financial assistance in different regions. Key components, such as the Employees Provident Fund, the Department of Social Welfare, the Social Security Organization and various healthcare subsidies, operate with limited coordination. The Independent Expert was informed that eligibility criteria, benefit structures and application procedures differed across programmes, making it challenging for older persons to identify their entitlements and how to have access to them. 29. The lack of an integrated approach leads to gaps in service delivery and inconsistent coverage, especially for older persons who do not enjoy formal employment during their working lives, such as informal workers and caregivers, particularly those from groups that suffer discrimination in access to the labour market, including older women, stateless persons, Indigenous persons andLGBTQI+ persons. Information about available schemes is often inaccessible and service providers are not always adequately trained in terms of being ableto offer coordinated referrals or support. As a result, many older persons remain unaware of the full range of benefits that they could have access to and are discouraged by bureaucratic hurdles. 30. Furthermore, many support schemes require complex documentation or digital literacy, potentially excluding older persons in the most vulnerable situations, especially those who are socially marginalized or lack family support. Social workers could be crucial in helping older persons to obtain benefits but the Independent Expert received information that there were not enough to support older persons. While thereare no official data on the exact number, the Malaysian Administrative Modernization and Management Planning Unit estimated in 2021 that there was one social worker for every 8,576 persons in Malaysia. Social work is not regulated or recognized as a profession by law, leading to a lack of adequate compensation, social recognition and understanding of the role of social workers. A social work profession bill, under development at the time of the visit, was expected to be tabled in 2025. The Independent Expert was not provided with a draft to review to ensure its alignment with international standards.

records.text: 24. Throughout the visit, government officials stated that families fulfilled the role of providing for older persons. While positive and caring family links are important and beneficial in a society, the well-being of older persons cannot be dependent only on the goodwill and resources of their families. In other words, family support systems cannot substitute for the Government’s responsibility in that regard. As stated in article 22 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, everyone, as a member of society, has the right to social security and is entitled to realization, through national effort and international co-operation and in accordance with the organization and resources of each State, of the economic, social and cultural rights indispensable for his dignity and the free development of his personality. In addition, article 25 provides that everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for the health and well-being of himself and of his family, including food, clothing, housing and medical care and necessary social services, and the right to security in the event of unemployment, sickness, disability, widowhood, old age or other lack of livelihood in circumstances beyond his control. The State, therefore, has a primary role in establishing a social security system to ensure that no older person is left without an income that guarantees the right to an adequate standard of living, irrespective of their family ties and the resources of their family, if they have one. 25. The contributory retirement income framework of Malaysia includes separate systems for private and public employees. While pensions for retired public employees are adequate, according to the information received, they are gradually being phased out and younger public employees can no longer opt in. Instead, they contribute to the Employees Provident Fund, the mandatory savings-based system also used by employees in the private sector. Participation in the Fund greatly facilitates a structured mechanism for building retirement savings but Fund officials acknowledged that there was a need to improve coverage, savings adequacy and the long-term sustainability of the system. Participating in the Fund did not guarantee an income that would allow retirees to enjoy an adequate standard of living. According to data provided by the Fund, only 36 per cent of its active members were currently meeting the saving targets that would allow them to fully finance their retirement needs. In addition, only 60 per cent of the labour force was currently covered by retirement and pension schemes (with the goal of 80 per cent coverage by 2035), and only 29 per cent of the older population was receiving a pension. The Fund was making efforts to widen its membership and had plans to include service and gig workers and migrants. The Government informed the Independent Expert that it intended to pass legislation introducing mandatory contributions to the Fund for migrant workers. 26. Currently, members of the Fund can withdraw their savings as a lump sum after the age of 55. That option has led to 25 per cent of retirees withdrawing their full savings from the Fund and exhausting them within five years after retirement, leaving them with no regular income. The option of a monthly payment instead of the withdrawal of a lump sum is currently not chosen by many members but, with an adequate monthly amount, would ensure a more sustainable income for retirees. That would require substantially increasing current regular contributions by most members. 27. Regarding non-contributory allowances (Bantuan Warga Emas and Bantuan Am, among others) for older persons, the system is complex and fragmented, making it difficult, even for the interlocutors met by the Independent Expert during her visit (activists, social workers, lawyers), to understand the variety of resources available and the different requirements for access to them. Public officials assured the Independent Expert that a wide network of government officials guaranteed effective government outreach to inform all of the eligible population. In remote rural areas, that was done through village leaders who met with government officials and then informed their communities. A simplified approach, however, would guarantee a minimum social protection floor to all older persons, making sure that none were left behind without the resources to sustain themselves.

records.text: 12. Ageism and age discrimination persist in Malaysia, according to the information received by the Independent Expert, with older Malaysians often encountering negative biases in such areas as the workplace and healthcare, as well as in society at large, yet ageism and age discrimination remain inadequately addressed in legal and policy frameworks. 13. During the visit, the Independent Expert heard the term “the elderly” when Government officials referred to older persons in English. In official documents, such as the National Policy for the Elderly, 1995, older persons used to be referred to as “warga tua” or “old citizens”. In 2011, in the updated National Policy, the term “warga emas” or “golden citizens” began to be used, which was perceived to be more dignified. While the Independent Expert understands that that choice was made to convey respect, it would be preferable to use the most objective possible term to refer to older persons in government documents and communications, such as “individu berumur” or “orang berumur”. That would follow the terminology used by the General Assembly since 1995. The term “older persons” highlights their individuality and avoids the negative connotations of “the elderly”, such as frailty, dependence or diminished value. The term “golden citizens” could have paternalistic or euphemistic connotations, which could potentially perpetuate ageist attitudes. 14. Malaysia has an extremely diverse society, which has enriched its culture, heritage and social and political life. That diversity is also reflected among its older population, which is as heterogeneous as the overall population. In order to fulfil the human rights of older persons, that diversity must be acknowledged and protected. Women, Indigenous persons, stateless persons and LGBTQI+ persons of older age shared compelling testimonies of intersecting forms of discrimination with the Independent Expert. The situation of older stateless persons is particularly urgent, as they are deprived of virtually all human rights, including their rights to freely move within the territory of Malaysia and have access to healthcare and employment. 15. The Independent Expert also noticed that many of the services offered to older persons were adapted to the majority population in the area that they served and lacked an inclusive approach. As an example, centres promoting social and cultural activities in Muslim-majority neighbourhoods had a strong religious component, becoming unappealing, in practice, to older persons in those areas who did not share the majority religion. 16. Ageism is prevalent in the labour market, according to information received during the visit. Many employers openly place age limits on recruitment, with advertisements for job offers excluding candidates above the age of 40. The mandatory retirement age of 60 (established by the Minimum Retirement Age Act 2012) means that many older persons are forced out of their jobs despite being willing and able to continue working. Those who seek new occupations after the age of 60, or even in their 50s, struggle to find employment. 17. That exclusion prevents Malaysia from benefiting from the wealth of experience that older persons offer. Furthermore, it affects the capacity of older persons to contribute to the economy and to receive an income that ensures their right to an adequate standard of living, especially in a context of insufficient pensions and social protection. 18. The Independent Expert has also received reports of age-based workplace discrimination, such as exclusion from training and development opportunities, preventing career growth, negative stereotypes, such as remarks that older persons lacked energy or technology skills or pressure “to take it easy”, and companies sometimes targeting senior employees for early retirement or retrenchment to cut costs, then rehiring them on less favourable terms. In the absence of legislation specifically banning that type of unequal treatment, the Government’s capacity to prevent it and of affected older persons to defend their rights in court are limited. 19. The Independent Expert welcomes that the Government and the private sector have adopted multiple initiatives to promote older persons’ right to work, including Daya Kerjaya, a programme that has facilitated the hiring of 6,638 persons above the age of 60 since 31December 2023, thanks to an incentive of 1,500 Malaysian ringgit (approximately $315) paid to the employer for a six-month period. Other initiatives include theIncome Tax (Deduction for Employment of Senior Citizen, Ex-Convict, Parolee, Supervised Person and Ex-Drug Dependent)Rules 2019 for employers who hire older persons earning 4,000 Malaysian ringgit (approximately $840 per month) or less. The MYFutureJobs platform, which connects older jobseekers with employers and training, has led to over 15,000 placements since 2020, according to government data. The Senior Back in Action programme has provided 6.94 million Malaysian ringgit (approximately $1.46 million) in financial aid to train nearly 2,000 older persons, while the TalentCorp programme offers such programmes as Career Comeback and Veteran MyWIRA, supporting older women and armed forces veterans, respectively, with skills development and reintegration into the workforce. Specialized job platforms for persons above 50 years of age, such as Hire. Seniors, have also been launched. The Malaysian Employers Federation has advocated for valuing the expertise of older persons and has suggested gradually raising the retirement age above 60 in response to the ageing workforce. 20. Officials of the Ministry of Human Resources told the Independent Expert that their policy was not to differentiate among older persons in terms of whether they were men, women, migrants or citizens. That approach, however, risked leaving behind groups affected by intersectional factors of discrimination, such as older women, older Indigenous persons, older migrants and older LGBTQI+ persons. Officials expressed their confidence that the general anti-discrimination legislation, the Employment Act 1955 (Act 265), as amended by the Employment (Amendment) Act 2022, and the Labour Court and the Industrial Court offered enough protection against those types of discrimination. Discrimination was not defined in the Employment Act, however, nor were specifically protected characteristics, such as age, gender, religion or sexual orientation, leaving room for interpretation. Officials stated that the courts had not received any complaints regarding gender discrimination in the workplace. 21. The Independent Expert noted that most government institutions did not collect or analyse data disaggregated by age group. Among those that did, some grouped together all persons above 55 years or 60 years and older, failing to address the disparities among persons in their 50s, 60s, 70s, 80s and beyond. That prevented an understanding of the extent of the social and economic gaps affecting older persons and could jeopardize the capacity to undertake legislative and policy actions to address them. 22. The Independent Expert was informed of a manifestation of discrimination against older persons in the private sphere: violence and abuse in family settings. Violence against older persons is one of the most underreported crimes globally, and a lack of awareness in Malaysian society and within the police and justice system in Malaysia prevents the reporting of more cases and, ultimately, a robust response to the issue. Older persons are protected under the Domestic Violence Act 1994 and general provisions of the Penal Code (Act 574) but, in practice, the number of cases addressed by institutions is very low. According to government data, the Department of Social Welfare acted on 159 cases over five years(2020–2024), an average of 31.8 cases per year. Compared to national and global estimates of the total number of cases, which range from 351,000 to 650,000 per year, only a small fraction of the issue is being addressed. 23. The Independent Expert received accounts of older persons becoming victims of abuse when they could no longer provide income to their families and started to be seen as a burden. Such cases remained largely underreported, according to testimonies and data received during the visit. As stated by the Government in 2023, the senior citizens bill may include a clause forcing relatives to support older persons under the threat of penalties, potentially exacerbating those tensions and increasing animosity towards economically vulnerable and dependent older persons.

records.text: 4. Malaysia is undergoing a demographic shift, with persons above the age of 65 constituting 11.6 per cent of the population (3.9 million) and projections indicating that, by 2030, that figure will have risen to 15.3 per cent (5.8 million). Malaysia became an ageing nation in 2020 and will be an aged nation by 2044 and a super-aged nation by 2056. The Government is aware of the shift and recognizes ageing as a priority, which constitutes a commendable starting point to adapt policies and legislation to the ageing population. The Independent Expert also noted multiple government initiatives to commence that adaptation. 5. Malaysia has ratified three of the core human rights treaties: the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, the Convention on the Rights of the Child, including the first two Optional Protocols thereto, and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. 6. Malaysia has not ratified core treaties that can contribute to the protection of the human rights of older persons, however, including the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination and the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families. Other instruments with a potential positive impact on the rights of older persons also remain unratified, including the Convention relating to the Status of Refugees, the Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons, the Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness and the Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention, 1989 (No. 169), of the International Labour Organization (ILO). 7. The Federal Constitution of Malaysia establishes the general human rights framework for the country. Article 8 (1) affirms the principle of equality before the law and affords equal protection of the law to all persons in Malaysia. Article 8 (2) prohibits discrimination on the grounds of religion, race, descent, place of birth or gender but does not explicitly prohibit discrimination based on age nor on other grounds, such as sexual orientation and identity or disability, which often intersect with age-based discrimination. 8. At the time of the visit, the Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development was drafting a senior citizens bill, which was expected to be presented in March 2025. Unfortunately, the Independent Expert did not have the opportunity to review a draft and make recommendations for its alignment with international standards. According to the information received, no meaningful participation or in-depth discussion of the draft had taken place with stakeholders at the time of the visit, nor had any information on its content been publicly disclosed. 9. The Government is currently implementing the Twelfth Malaysia Plan, a socioeconomic development plan for the period 2021–2025, and designing the Thirteenth Malaysia Plan for the period 2026–2030. The Twelfth Malaysia Plan includes references to older persons in several contexts. In relation to healthcare, it contains an emphasis on the need to address the demographic shift by strengthening financing, public awareness and technological solutions. Regarding social protection, it contains a long-term care framework that includes the enhancement of pension and retirement systems. Also mentioned are senior-friendly communities and lifelong learning to empower older persons and their social participation. 10. The National Policy for Older Persons of Malaysia, which is under the responsibility of the Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development, was introduced in 1995 and revised in 2011. It is aimed at promoting the well-being, dignity and active participation of older persons and contains an emphasis on health and well-being, inclusion and participation, security and protection and enabling environments and infrastructure. 11. Most officials with whom the Independent Expert met were aware of the demographic shift and the urgency of adapting government action to the changing situation. Most authorities stated that ageing constituted a top priority and shared targeted initiatives and programmes specifically addressing older persons. Efforts to address the nation’s ageing, however, were disparate among different ministries and departments at the federal and state levels and lacked a coordinated, systematic approach, despite the existence of the National Action Plan for Senior Citizens.

records.text: 55. Recalling its previous recommendation (see CEDAW/C/MYS/CO/3-5 , para. 54) and its general recommendation No. 29 (2013) on the economic consequences of marriage, family relations and their dissolution, the Committee recommends that the State party: (a) Harmonize national legislation and Sharia law with the Convention, ensuring that any conflict of law with regard to women’s equal rights in marriage and family relations, divorce and to inheritance is resolved in full compliance with the Convention. In that regard, it recommends that the State party engage in discussions with leaders of religious communities, religious scholars and women’s rights groups, taking into consideration best practices in the region and in other member States of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation; (b) Ensure women’s equal right to enter into marriage on their own accord by abolishing the requirement of the permission of a male guardian; (c) Ensure that both parents are recognized as legal guardians of the child and that women have equal rights as men with regard to divorce, matrimonial property and inheritance; (d) Remove restrictions on interfaith marriages and decriminalize extramarital sex as well as pregnancy and childbirth out of wedlock to respect women’s agency to make their autonomous sexual and reproductive choices; (e) Prohibit polygamy, in law and in practice, raise awareness about its harmful effects on women, in line with the Committee’s general recommendation No. 21 (1994) on equality in marriage and family relations and joint general recommendation No. 31 of the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women/general comment No. 18 of the Committee on the Rights of the Child (2019) on harmful practices, as revised, and ensure the protection of the economic rights of women and their children in existing polygamous unions and upon their dissolution.

The Committee recommends that, in line with its general recommendations No. 37 (2018) on the gender-related dimensions of disaster risk reduction in the context of climate change and No. 39 (2022) on the rights of Indigenous women and girls, the State party review its climate change and disaster response strategies, taking into account the negative effects of climate change on the livelihoods of women, especially rural and Indigenous women, and ensure that women are meaningfully involved in the development, adoption and implementation of legislation, policies and programmes on climate change, disaster response and disaster risk reduction by, in particular: (a) Collecting disaggregated data on the impact of climate change and natural disasters on women and girls, including rural and Indigenous women and girls; (b) Ensuring the incorporation of a gender perspective in climate change and disaster risk reduction strategies, renewable energy legislation, financing and programmes in order to address the specific and unique needs of women and girls and build their resilience and effective adaptation to climate change; (c) Taking measures to address the specific impact of climate change on women’s livelihoods and access to resources, and ensuring their economic empowerment in the transition to a green economy.
